title: A neighbor's day of atonement
hook: Jews keep Yom Kippur as a day of fasting and repentance, in their own way and with their own meaning

segments.voice: Yesterday: the spring equinox, aequinoctium, and a scale that's never perfectly even. Your line was equal light. Did one small thing move across to the lighter side? Day six hundred sixty-eight.

One autumn evening, synagogues fill for a day the Torah sets apart. Some people wear white. Those who keep the fast eat nothing and drink nothing from that evening until the stars come out the next night, when a long blast of the ram's horn ends the day. This is Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. Leviticus calls it a sabbath of solemn rest. It isn't ours to borrow. But a good neighbor can learn what it is, and let it ask a question of their own life.
screen: `AN AUTUMN EVENING, SYNAGOGUES FILL.` → `EVENING TO NIGHTFALL, NO FOOD OR WATER.` → `A NEIGHBOR'S HOLY DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the source. In the book of Leviticus, the tenth day of the seventh month is set apart. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, the people are told: "ye shall afflict your souls." Jewish tradition has long understood that as fasting and holding back from certain comforts, and the day is spent largely in prayer, from the evening service called Kol Nidre to the closing service, Neilah. Second, the inner work. The Hebrew word at its center is teshuvah, often translated repentance, though it comes from the root for returning. Turning back. Jewish teachers, Maimonides among them, describe recognizing a wrong, regretting it, setting it right where possible, and resolving to do differently. Third, a teaching about other people. The Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish law, says Yom Kippur brings atonement for wrongs between a person and God, but for wrongs between one person and another, not until you've made peace with the person you wronged. So it's a custom, in the days before it, to call, write and apologize. The day doesn't skip the phone call. Fourth, what a neighbor can take, carefully. Not the fast, not the prayers, not the meaning, which belong to the people who keep it. Only the question it leaves in the air for anyone watching with respect: have I looked honestly at my year? Is there someone I owe a word to? The Stoics had their own version, Seneca's nightly review, which we'll meet again soon. That nightly look is a different thing, from a different place, and it doesn't stand in for this one.
screen: `LEVITICUS: YE SHALL AFFLICT YOUR SOULS.` · `TESHUVAH: TURNING BACK.` · `WRONGED A PERSON? MAKE PEACE FIRST.` · `A NEIGHBOR'S QUESTION, NOT A BORROWING.` · then, large: `HONEST REVIEW.`

segments.voice: In your own way, look back over the past year. Not to punish yourself. Just to see. Where did you do well? Let that count. Where did you fall short of who you meant to be? Name one place, plainly. Is there a person connected to it? If there is, picture them, and ask whether a word from you, an apology or a thank-you, might be owed. You don't have to decide now. Just let the honest picture stand. The bell holds the time.
Teshuvah, the Hebrew word at the heart of Yom Kippur, meaning turning back: recognizing a wrong, regretting it, and resolving to do differently. Today's word.
Your line: honest review. If one person came to mind in the practice, consider sending them a short, honest message today. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: On Yom Kippur many Jews fast from one evening until nightfall the next and spend much of the day in synagogue prayer; in the days before it, many seek out people they have wronged to apologize.

original.note: Hebrew: the Day of Atonement (in the Bible, yom ha-kippurim).

trapdoor: what you thought: a day of atonement is about feeling sorry.
what it means: Yom Kippur is a day of fasting, prayer and teshuvah, turning back, including making peace with people.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 16:29–31 and 23:27 set the day; Mishnah Yoma 8:9 separates sins against God from sins against a fellow person, which need the person's forgiveness.

sources.ref: Letters to Lucilius; On Anger 3.36 (Seneca's nightly review)

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut the unsourced superlative 'the most solemn day of the Jewish year' (now Leviticus 16:31's own 'a sabbath of solemn rest'), the 'twenty-five hours' count (now Leviticus 23:32's evening to evening), 'synagogues fill past capacity / people who rarely come', and 'many Jews call, write and apologize' (now described as a custom); the four steps attributed to Jewish teachers such as Maimonides; cut the empty closing line 'many paths ... ask for an honest look'. Replaced the 25-hour myth item.
Leviticus 16:29 JPS 1917 phrase 'ye shall afflict your souls': confirm exact wording.
Teshuvah from the root shuv, to return; the four steps (recognition, regret, repair, resolve) are a common summary drawing on Maimonides, Laws of Repentance 2. Confirm framing.
Fast length about 25 hours; white clothing customary for many; shofar blast at the end of Neilah. Confirm general accuracy.
